rounds.proof_sketch: Block size is fixed at 256, so threadIdx.x ∈ [0,255]. All shared_mem accesses are shared_mem[tid] or shared_mem[tid+stride] where tid<stride. Maximum access: when tid=127, stride=128 → index 255. With input size=128, num_blocks=1. The element at index 256 in the mutant is never accessed regardless of input values.
rounds.survival_reason: The mutation changes shared memory allocation from 256 to 257 floats, but this extra element is never accessed. The kernel uses block_size=256, meaning threadIdx.x ranges from 0-255, and shared_mem[tid] only accesses indices 0-255. The parallel reduction loop accesses shared_mem[tid+stride] where tid<stride, with maximum index being 127+128=255 when stride=128. Since no code path ever reads or writes to index 256, the mutation is semantically invisible to all possible input values. This is a purely structural difference in memory allocation that cannot be exposed through value-level testing.
rounds.kill_strategy: Unkillable under fixed-shape contract. The mutation only allocates one extra unused shared memory float. To kill this mutant would require either: (1) changing block_size to >256 so threads could access index 256, or (2) modifying the kernel code to access the 257th element. Neither is possible under the value-level testing contract.
rounds.recommendations: Mutation testing tools should classify shared memory size increases (where the additional memory is provably unreachable) as equivalent mutations. A static analysis pass checking maximum shared memory index against allocation size could automatically identify such unkillable mutants without requiring extensive dynamic testing.
